s00_title
Riffle. An explainable AI co-pilot for citizen stream science. Built for the IEEE OneAquaHealth Global Hackathon, track three: AI-supported assessment.
s01_home

Urban streams can turn dangerous within hours, after a sewer overflow or a summer algal bloom. Yet they are monitored only a few times a year. Riffle lets any neighbour check a stream in five minutes, with an AI co-pilot that double-checks with them, not instead of them. And it turns every observation into One Health insight and early warning.
s02_today

The home screen answers the question people actually have: is my stream OK today? At the Vale das Flores park outlet, the latest check found no animals in warm, green water, so Riffle advises keeping dogs on the lead. The three rings are the One Health reading: ecosystem, people, and animals.
s03_water

Let's do a check. Everything is plain language and pictures, with no jargon. The water here is murky and grey, with a sewage smell. Then a quick look at the banks: plants, shade, litter, and any pipes discharging into the stream.
s04_bugs

Now the bug hunt. Riffle uses the miniSASS biomonitoring method. Every animal group has a how-to-tell guide with its key identification features, and there is a built-in five-minute sampling timer. I'll record stoneflies and flat mayflies, which are very sensitive to pollution, plus some worms.
s05_copilot

This is the heart of Riffle. Only now, after I've recorded my animals, does the co-pilot reveal its expectation, so it can't bias what I see. A transparent model predicts the score a stream that looks like this should have, and shows exactly which observations drove it. It raises two questions: an expert rule says stoneflies rarely survive sewage, and the model says my animals score higher than expected.
s06_decide

I'm the scientist here. I can go back and check, or confirm with a note. I counted two tails, so I confirm. Because the question stays open, the record is published as preliminary, and sent to a local expert.
s07_result

I get a One Health reading with practical advice, experience points that reward careful science, and new badges. And the same check becomes an HL7 FHIR R4 bundle: observations, the co-pilot's flags as detected issues, and provenance recording what the citizen, the AI, and the expert each contributed. It validates live.
s08_review

In the expert review queue, experts see the citizen's note next to the model's evidence, and verify or reject in seconds. Riffle also tracks how often flagged records turn out to be valid. That is how we audit the AI itself.
s09_map
For cities, the map shows stream health, or seven-day risk, across Coimbra, and ranks what is stressing the streams most: a to-do list for the municipality.
s10_site

On the urban reach of the Coselhas stream, the trend shows the decline since construction began upstream. This presence map shows sensitive insects disappearing, quarter by quarter: an early warning sign in itself.
s11_alerts

Early warning combines the live Open-Meteo forecast with each site's vulnerability and the latest citizen observations, covering sewer overflow, heat and algal blooms, and flash floods. Here is the storm and heatwave stress test, with the affected sites and concrete actions for people and pet owners.
s12_learn
To build awareness, a storytelling module follows one raindrop from city rooftops to a poisoned dog, and a glossary translates scientific jargon into plain words.
s13_data

Finally, open data and standards: bulk FHIR and CSV export, the architecture, and a model card that documents exactly how the AI works, and where its limits are. Everything runs on the device, works offline, and needs no account.
s14_end
Riffle. From streams to systems. Try it now at karan6705 dot github dot io slash riffle.
